title: Calculate the difference in days between two employees' joining dates using `ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(...)`.
shortTitle: Calculate the difference in days between two employees' joining dates using ChronoUnit.DAYS.between

s1_definition.profdef: `ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(startDate, endDate)` returns the number of whole days between two `LocalDate` values as a long. It is positive when end is after start and negative when end is before start.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya wants to know how many days apart two employees joined. She counts the days from the earlier joining date to the later one.
s1_definition.oneliner: `ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(d1, d2)` gives the whole-day gap — negative if d2 is before d1.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(startDate, endDate)` returns the number of whole days between two `LocalDate` values as a long. It is positive when end is after start and negative when end is before start.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Priya wants to know how many days apart two employees joined. She counts the days from the earlier joining date to the later one.

**One line to remember:** `ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(d1, d2)` gives the whole-day gap — negative if d2 is before d1.

sections.s2_technical:
`ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(a, b)` computes the signed count of complete days from a to b. For example between 2020-01-01 and 2020-01-15 it returns 14, and reversing the arguments returns minus 14. It works on any Temporal that supports days, including LocalDate, and correctly spans months and leap years.

If you want the absolute gap regardless of order you wrap the result in `Math.abs`. ChronoUnit also offers WEEKS, MONTHS, and YEARS for other granularities, all using the same between method. Because LocalDate is zone-free, the day count is purely calendar-based with no daylight-saving complications.

The senior nuance is choosing ChronoUnit.DAYS.between over Period for a plain day count — Period gives a years-months-days breakdown, whereas ChronoUnit gives a single total in the chosen unit, which is what "difference in days" means. I guard against null dates and decide whether I want the signed or absolute difference based on the business meaning, since a signed value tells me the order while an absolute value only tells me the gap.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India compares two employees' seniority by computing how many days apart they joined.

This is exactly what ChronoUnit DAYS between does — it returns the whole-day gap between the two joining dates.

The code defines a `SeniorityService.daysBetweenJoining` method and a demo.
sections.s5_journey:
Input: Rajesh joined 2020-01-01 and Priya joined 2020-03-01.

Step 1: ChronoUnit DAYS between of Rajesh's date and Priya's date counts the whole days from January 1 to March 1.

Step 2: January has 31 days and February 2020 has 29 (leap year), so the count is 60.

Step 3: Because Priya's date is after Rajesh's, the signed result is positive 60.

Step 4: Math.abs leaves 60 unchanged, giving the absolute gap.

```
INFO: Signed (Rajesh → Priya): 60 days
INFO: Absolute gap           : 60 days
```


sections.s6_takeaway:
To find the number of days between two joining dates I use ChronoUnit dot DAYS dot between, passing the start date and the end date. It returns the count of whole days as a long, positive when the end date is after the start and negative when it is before, and it correctly spans months and leap years because the java dot time API models the real calendar. Between the first of January and the first of March 2020 it returns sixty, since that February had twenty-nine days.

At the National Bank of India I use this to compare seniority by the day gap between two employees' joining dates. When I only care about how far apart they are regardless of who joined first, I wrap the result in Math dot abs to get the absolute gap; when the order matters, I keep the signed value because its sign tells me which employee joined earlier.

The senior point I stress is choosing ChronoUnit dot DAYS dot between over Period for this. Period gives a years-months-days breakdown, which answers a different question, whereas the phrase "difference in days" means a single total in days, which is exactly what ChronoUnit returns. I also guard against null dates and decide up front whether the signed or absolute difference matches the business meaning.
